power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 5 codebook/README/label sources and 758 data columns across 63 files.
No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.
#### Duplicated Column Names

- **Duplicated column names in `rh.Yeo_Brainmap_10to14Comp_TopSpecializationComp.csv`.** 1 column name appears more than once (worst: `Top Component`×5), so 5 of the file's 10 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

- **Duplicated column names in `lh.Yeo_Brainmap_10to14Comp_TopSpecializationComp.csv`.** 1 column name appears more than once (worst: `Top Component`×5), so 5 of the file's 10 columns share a name with another. #### Files that do not belong in the repository

We left out 1644 files that software creates by itself, not the authors: editor backups (9), operating system (1635). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. A `.gitignore` based on GitHub's templates (https://github.com/github/gitignore) keeps them out of a repository.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 793 columns across 70 data files.
#### Issues Identified

16 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 70 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

This module also assesses whether the paper's Python code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 32 Python code files.

#### File paths
**3 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `greedy_forward_r2_train.csv` to `../../data/interim/results/behavioral/greedy_forward_r2_train.csv` (in dimension_analysis.py); `greedy_forward_r2_train.csv` to `../data/interim/results/behavioral/greedy_forward_r2_train.csv` (in regen_contrastive_grid_all.py); `greedy_forward_r2_train.csv` to `../data/interim/results/behavioral/greedy_forward_r2_train.csv` (in regen_top10_cloudmatched.py). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files. 7 references matched several files sharing a name and could not be resolved by study group or folder; they were left unrewritten and flagged.
#### Execution
**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 32 scripts: 16 ran without error, 5 errored, 2 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. 8 files were not run on their own, because other files import them: config.py (by dim_selection_train.py, explained_variance.py, explained_variance_shared_only.py, split_half_reliability_corrected.py, behavioral_contrastive_captions.py, dimension_analysis.py, dimension_interpretation.py, refit_contrastive_grid.py, regen_contrastive_grid_all.py, regen_top10_cloudmatched.py, make_paper_figures.py, download_fmri.py, neural_explained_variance.py, neural_explained_variance_per_subject.py, neural_rsa.py, plot_combined_surfaces_pair.py, plot_per_subject_searchlight.py, searchlight_behavioral_rsa.py, searchlight_rsa.py, dimension_recoverability.py, dimension_recoverability_hebart.py, fractionation_across_seeds.py, plot_fractionation_summary.py, surfaces.py, variance_partition.py, train_embedding_model.py); action_categories.py (by explained_variance.py, explained_variance_shared_only.py, dimension_analysis.py, neural_explained_variance.py, neural_explained_variance_per_subject.py, searchlight_behavioral_rsa.py); data_helpers.py (by dimension_recoverability.py, train_embedding_model.py); pub_style.py (by make_paper_figures.py); reliability.py (by dim_selection_train.py, explained_variance.py, explained_variance_shared_only.py); surfaces.py (by plot_combined_surfaces_pair.py, plot_per_subject_searchlight.py, searchlight_behavioral_rsa.py, searchlight_rsa.py); variance_partition.py (by explained_variance.py, explained_variance_shared_only.py, neural_explained_variance.py, neural_explained_variance_per_subject.py); video_bootstrap.py (by explained_variance_shared_only.py). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a `requirements.txt`). **1 script stopped on a file another script writes**, so it was run once more after the other scripts: `regen_contrastive_grid_all.py` (greedy_forward_r2_train.csv). Then this one ran to the end: `regen_contrastive_grid_all.py`. Which script must run first can be stated in a README, or shown by numbering the file names (01_, 02_). **2 scripts looked for 2 files in another folder than the deposit has them**, so before running them once more we copied them there: `data/interim/results/behavioral/greedy_forward_r2_train.csv` to `data/interim/data/interim/results/behavioral/greedy_forward_r2_train.csv` for `dimension_analysis.py`; `data/interim/results/behavioral/greedy_forward_r2_train.csv` to `data/interim/results/data/interim/results/behavioral/greedy_forward_r2_train.csv` for `regen_top10_cloudmatched.py`. Building paths from the top of the project (as with `here::here()`), or keeping the folders the code expects, solves this. **1 script needs the internet**, which is off during the run: download_fmri.py. text.text: How does the human mind organize dynamic social scenes?

Existing accounts rely on pre-defined social-affective or action-based taxonomies, yet whether humans use these dimensions to structure their representations of naturalistic social scenes remains unknown.
We collected 53,223 human similarity judgments of videos depicting two-person actions and trained a sparse-positive-embedding model to recover the underlying latent dimensions.

These learned dimensions explained twice as much variance in similarity judgments as pre-labeled annotations, captured interpretable fine-grained social-event structure (combining information about social relationships and actions), and fractionated broad semantic content (e.g., separating parent-child interactions into caregiving versus affectionate play).
The same dimensions also predicted fMRI responses to passively viewed stimuli across visual cortex better than pre-labeled annotations, highlighting their importance beyond similarity judgments.

Together, these results suggest that humans represent dynamic social scenes along fine-grained axes not captured by current taxonomies, and offer behaviorally-grounded targets for future studies of social vision.
Humans rapidly extract rich social structure from a brief, dynamic visual scene: who is present, what they are doing, how they relate to one another, and what kind of situation is unfolding.
This ability allows people to anticipate what others will do and decide whether and how to engage with them.
Yet we know surprisingly little about the representational organization of social scene perception.
Existing theories make different predictions about this organization.
Social and affective theories emphasize evaluations of individuals and relationships along broad dimensions like warmth, dominance, valence, and arousal [1] [2] [3] [4] .
text.formatted: Social and affective theories emphasize evaluations of individuals and relationships along broad dimensions like warmth, dominance, valence, and arousal <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">[1]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">[2]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">[3]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">[4]</ref> .

text.text: In contrast, a large body of research has focused on the visual nature of recognizing short, de-contextualized social events with action-centered theories that emphasize event labels and action categories [5] or along action-related dimensions like whether actions are directed towards people or objects [6, 7] .
text.formatted: In contrast, a large body of research has focused on the visual nature of recognizing short, de-contextualized social events with action-centered theories that emphasize event labels and action categories <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> or along action-related dimensions like whether actions are directed towards people or objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7]</ref> .

text.text: More recent work has extended these to also describe relational cues about bodies and their interactions [8] [9] [10] .
text.formatted: More recent work has extended these to also describe relational cues about bodies and their interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">[9]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10]</ref> .

text.text: Recognizing these short social events is supported in lateral occipital regions of visual cortex, with increasing sensitivity to social information along a lateral visual pathway [11] [12] [13] .
text.formatted: Recognizing these short social events is supported in lateral occipital regions of visual cortex, with increasing sensitivity to social information along a lateral visual pathway <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">[11]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">[13]</ref> .

text.text: This visual information about bodies and their actions and interactions is thought to be largely separate from higher-level social-affective information represented in higher-order regions such as the default mode network [8] .
text.formatted: This visual information about bodies and their actions and interactions is thought to be largely separate from higher-level social-affective information represented in higher-order regions such as the default mode network <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> .

text.text: These frameworks have been productive, and though they differ in their proposed organizing principles, they share a common limitation: the candidate dimensions are specified before the representational space is measured, leaving open the question of whether human observers organize complex social scenes along different, unanticipated dimensions.
Data-driven similarity methods provide a complementary route, building on the long-standing use of similarity as a window onto mental representation [14] [15] [16] .
text.formatted: Data-driven similarity methods provide a complementary route, building on the long-standing use of similarity as a window onto mental representation <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[14]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[15]</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">[16]</ref> .

text.text: Rather than beginning with pre-labeled taxonomies, these models infer the representational structure directly from human similarity judgments.

In other rich domains including objects [17] , reachable spaces [18] , materials [19] , and actions [20, 21] , large-scale similarity judgments have been used to learn sparse representational spaces directly from behavior.
text.formatted: In other rich domains including objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> , reachable spaces <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">[18]</ref> , materials <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[19]</ref> , and actions <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21]</ref> , large-scale similarity judgments have been used to learn sparse representational spaces directly from behavior.

text.text: These approaches can recover interpretable structure that predefined taxonomies and existing labels miss; and in the object domain, these behavior-derived dimensions have proven to do a better job at predicting neural responses to images of objects than category models [22] .
text.formatted: These approaches can recover interpretable structure that predefined taxonomies and existing labels miss; and in the object domain, these behavior-derived dimensions have proven to do a better job at predicting neural responses to images of objects than category models <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[22]</ref> .

text.text: Dynamic social scenes, however, present a qualitatively different and understudied representational problem.
Unlike isolated objects or actions, they simultaneously contain information about people, actions, relations, and social-affective content.
A crying infant being comforted, bathed, or consoled contains many of the same agents and objects yet these scenes constitute semantically and socially distinct situations.

It is therefore unknown whether social-scene similarity can be reduced to familiar visual, relational, action or social-semantic categories, or instead reflects richer, context-dependent situational structure.
Here we use large-scale similarity judgments and a data driven approach to ask how humans organize dynamic social scenes.

We collected 49,484 odd-one-out triplet similarity judgments from 215 participants on a dataset of short, naturalistic social videos [12] (Fig. 1a), and trained a sparse positive similarity embedding (SPoSE) [17, 23] to recover the latent geometry of these judgments (Fig. 1b).
text.formatted: We collected 49,484 odd-one-out triplet similarity judgments from 215 participants on a dataset of short, naturalistic social videos <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1a</ref>), and trained a sparse positive similarity embedding (SPoSE) <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">23]</ref> to recover the latent geometry of these judgments (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1b</ref>).

text.text: We find a relatively compact embedding space explains roughly twice as much variance in 3,739 heldout similarity judgments (17 different participants) compared to the combination of pre-labeled annotations based on prior theories of visual, action-related, and socialaffective information, using multiple regression representational similarity analysis (RSA) [24, 25] (Fig. 1c).
text.formatted: We find a relatively compact embedding space explains roughly twice as much variance in 3,739 heldout similarity judgments (17 different participants) compared to the combination of pre-labeled annotations based on prior theories of visual, action-related, and socialaffective information, using multiple regression representational similarity analysis (RSA) <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25]</ref> (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1c</ref>).

text.text: These behaviorally derived dimensions also predict fMRI representational geometry, substantially better than the pre-labeled annotations previously used to characterize this pathway on the same data, across the visual cortex, including the lateral stream and STS.

Together, these findings suggest that human social vision is organized not by the conventional social-affective dimensions or action categories alone, but by a richer representational geometry in which information about actions and social relationships is combined in ways that are not fully captured by prior taxonomies.

To understand the representations humans use to organize social scenes, we collected odd-one-out triplet similarity judgments from 215 participants on an existing dataset of 250 naturalistic social interaction videos depicting two people in everyday actions, with accompanying human behavior annotations and fMRI responses. [12] These prelabeled behavior annotations were collected based on prior theories of action and interaction representations, [12] and were grouped into the following broad categories: • Visual features of the scene: spatial expanse (whether the video depicts a closeup or large, expansive scene) and indoor/outdoor (whether the video takes place indoors or outdoors).
text.formatted: To understand the representations humans use to organize social scenes, we collected odd-one-out triplet similarity judgments from 215 participants on an existing dataset of 250 naturalistic social interaction videos depicting two people in everyday actions, with accompanying human behavior annotations and fMRI responses. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> These prelabeled behavior annotations were collected based on prior theories of action and interaction representations, <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> and were grouped into the following broad categories: • Visual features of the scene: spatial expanse (whether the video depicts a closeup or large, expansive scene) and indoor/outdoor (whether the video takes place indoors or outdoors).

text.text: • Visuospatial configuration of bodies: inter-agent distance (the distance between the people) and agents facing (the extent to which the two people in the video are facing each other).

• Actions and social interactions: action category (the semantic action category labels released with the Moments in Time dataset [5] ), object-directed (the extent to which an action was directed at an object), acting jointly (the extent to which the two people were interacting physically) and communicative interactions (the extent to which the two people were communicating).
text.formatted: • Actions and social interactions: action category (the semantic action category labels released with the Moments in Time dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> ), object-directed (the extent to which an action was directed at an object), acting jointly (the extent to which the two people were interacting physically) and communicative interactions (the extent to which the two people were communicating).

text.text: • Social-affective features of the relationship: intimacy (how intimate the people in the video appear), dominance (whether one person appears dominant over the other), cooperation (the extent to which the people in the video appear to be cooperating), valence (how positive or negative the interaction appears) and arousal (how intense or energetic the interaction appears).

Pre-labeled annotations were collected in an online experiment [12] where at least 10 human subjects rated each feature for each video on a five-point Likert scale, with the exception of indoor/outdoor (binary label) and action category (pre-classified).
text.formatted: Pre-labeled annotations were collected in an online experiment <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> where at least 10 human subjects rated each feature for each video on a five-point Likert scale, with the exception of indoor/outdoor (binary label) and action category (pre-classified).

text.text: We collected an additional 3,739 held-out similarity judgments from 17 participants on a 50-video subset of the 250 videos to use for evaluation.
The similarity data was reliable across participants (held-out 50-video test set; noise ceiling r² = 0.67, Spearman-Brown corrected split-half reliability over 1,000 splits).
We first asked how well the above pre-labeled annotations explained human similarity judgments.
For each annotation, we constructed a representational similarity matrix (RSM) and conducted cross-validated, multiple regression RSA to predict the held-out human similarity data.
Individually, only a few features explained significant variance in similarity judgments: dominance, spatial expanse and intimacy.

Further, the full model combining all the pre-labeled annotations explained only r² = 0.25 of held-out human similarity structure, compared with a split-half reliability estimate of r² = 0.67 (Fig. 2a).
text.formatted: Further, the full model combining all the pre-labeled annotations explained only r² = 0.25 of held-out human similarity structure, compared with a split-half reliability estimate of r² = 0.67 (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2a</ref>).

text.text: Thus, while pre-labeled annotations based on prior theories captured meaningful structure, they left most of the reliable variance in human judgments unexplained.

To close this gap in explaining behavioral similarity judgments, we learned a sparse positive embedding directly from the triplet judgments, using the SPoSE model of Hebart et al. [17] Briefly, this model represents each video as a point in a sparse, nonnegative embedding space, where the embedding dimensions are learned by predicting which video participants chose as the odd one out.
text.formatted: To close this gap in explaining behavioral similarity judgments, we learned a sparse positive embedding directly from the triplet judgments, using the SPoSE model of Hebart et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> Briefly, this model represents each video as a point in a sparse, nonnegative embedding space, where the embedding dimensions are learned by predicting which video participants chose as the odd one out.

text.text: An L1 penalty encourages sparse, interpretable dimensions (Methods, Section 4.3).
After training and pruning negligible dimensions, the model retained 40 non-zero dimensions.

The 40 learned dimensions explained r² = 0.51 (95% CI [0.36, 0.59]) of the held-out human similarity matrix, roughly twice the variance explained by the pre-labeled annotation model (difference = 0.26, 95% CI [0.10, 0.37]; Fig. 2b).
text.formatted: The 40 learned dimensions explained r² = 0.51 (95% CI [0.36, 0.59]) of the held-out human similarity matrix, roughly twice the variance explained by the pre-labeled annotation model (difference = 0.26, 95% CI [0.10, 0.37]; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2b</ref>).

text.text: Variance partitioning demonstrates that the prelabeled annotations add only a small amount of unique explainable variance beyond the learned dimensions (unique r² = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.06]), while the learned dimensions explain substantial unique variance (unique r² = 0.29, 95% CI [0.13, 0.38]; Fig. 2c).
text.formatted: Variance partitioning demonstrates that the prelabeled annotations add only a small amount of unique explainable variance beyond the learned dimensions (unique r² = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.02, 0.06]), while the learned dimensions explain substantial unique variance (unique r² = 0.29, 95% CI [0.13, 0.38]; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2c</ref>).

text.text: These results suggest that human social scene similarity judgments contain much more structure than pre-labeled feature taxonomies capture.
To characterize the learned representation, we ranked dimensions by their incremental contribution to cross-validated prediction of the training similarity structure (Methods, Section 4.3).
A greedy forward-selection curve showed diminishing returns as dimensions were added, with an elbow at 11 dimensions identified by the Kneedle algorithm [26] (Extended Data Fig. 1).
text.formatted: A greedy forward-selection curve showed diminishing returns as dimensions were added, with an elbow at 11 dimensions identified by the Kneedle algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> (Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref>).

text.text: These 11 dimensions accounted for most of the full embedding's predictive performance (r2 ≈ 0.41, or 79% of the full 40-dimension model's r² = 0.51; Fig. 2b).
text.formatted: These 11 dimensions accounted for most of the full embedding's predictive performance (r2 ≈ 0.41, or 79% of the full 40-dimension model's r² = 0.51; Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2b</ref>).

text.text: We therefore use the reduced set of 11 dimensions as a descriptive subset for illustration and interpretation, not as evidence that the psychological representation has exactly 11 discrete or immutable dimensions.
We note, however, that all 11 dimensions were stable across bootstrap resamples and random initializations (mean reliability 0.60-0.88; Extended Data Fig. 2a).
text.formatted: We note, however, that all 11 dimensions were stable across bootstrap resamples and random initializations (mean reliability 0.60-0.88; Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2a</ref>).

text.text: The top dimensions depicted themes including adult conversation in cars (Dim 1), infant caregiving (Dim 0), outdoor activities (Dim 13), martial arts and sports (Dim 7), infants crying (Dim 9), people playing music (Dim 2), playful parent-child interaction (Dim 4), children dancing and playing (Dim 3), cooking and eating (Dim 6), sports (Dim 17), and infant play and bath contexts (Dim 8) (Fig. 3; all dimensions in Extended Data Fig. 3).
text.formatted: The top dimensions depicted themes including adult conversation in cars (Dim 1), infant caregiving (Dim 0), outdoor activities (Dim 13), martial arts and sports (Dim 7), infants crying (Dim 9), people playing music (Dim 2), playful parent-child interaction (Dim 4), children dancing and playing (Dim 3), cooking and eating (Dim 6), sports (Dim 17), and infant play and bath contexts (Dim 8) (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>; all dimensions in Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>).

text.text: To interpret the content of the dimensions, we performed a caption analysis identifying the most contrastive words for each dimension, that is, words present in captions for videos with high but not low loadings (Methods, Section 4.6).
The resulting word clouds (Fig. 3) showed that each dimension was associated with a coherent set of semantically related words.
text.formatted: The resulting word clouds (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3</ref>) showed that each dimension was associated with a coherent set of semantically related words.

text.text: Across the top 11 dimensions, the contrastive vocabulary of high-loading videos diverged from that of low-loading videos more than expected for random groups of videos (Jensen-Shannon divergence 0.72-0.80 bits versus a chance level of 0.61 bits, p < 0.05, FDR-corrected; Extended Data Table 1), indicating that each dimension captures specific semantic content.
text.formatted: Across the top 11 dimensions, the contrastive vocabulary of high-loading videos diverged from that of low-loading videos more than expected for random groups of videos (Jensen-Shannon divergence 0.72-0.80 bits versus a chance level of 0.61 bits, p < 0.05, FDR-corrected; Extended Data Table <ref type="table">1</ref>), indicating that each dimension captures specific semantic content.

text.text: The contrastive vocabulary describes most dimensions as blending information about people or groups of people, and their actions (e.g., Dim 0: 'baby', 'feed', 'brush'; Dim 2: 'band', 'drum', 'sing', 'guitar'; Dim 3: 'girl', 'child', 'dance').
We note that the stimuli all depict two person videos, while the caption analysis reduced captions to common single-word base (e.g., babies to baby, playing to play).
While some dimensions were characterized by non-social activities taking place (e.g., Dim 13: 'fish', 'person', 'dog'), the majority of dimensions depict distinct social scenes and relationships.
A particularly striking property of the learned dimensions is that related semantic content is often fractionated rather than represented in a single dimension.
Infantrelated videos, for example, load on separable dimensions associated with caregiving routines (Dim 0: feeding, brushing) versus playful interaction (Dims 4 and 8).
Playbased interactions are separated by the people in the video and their social relationship into parent-child (Dim 4) versus child-child (Dim 8), even though the top verb for both is 'play'.
Similarly, adult dyadic scenes separate into conversation (Dim 1), cooking and eating (Dim 6), sport and other situational regimes.

These dimensions are correlated (Extended Data Fig. 4) and sometimes map onto more general semantic or event distinctions (for example, driving versus cooking), but they capture distinct relational and affective structures.
text.formatted: These dimensions are correlated (Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>) and sometimes map onto more general semantic or event distinctions (for example, driving versus cooking), but they capture distinct relational and affective structures.

text.text: This fractionation is also reproducible: it occurs at least once in 19 of 20 retrains of the embedding.

The specific dimensions that fractionate vary across retrains (Extended Data Fig. 2b); they most often resemble outdoor activity (10 of 20 retrains), caregiving (9 of 20), conversation (6 of 20) and musical performance (4 of 20).
text.formatted: The specific dimensions that fractionate vary across retrains (Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2b</ref>); they most often resemble outdoor activity (10 of 20 retrains), caregiving (9 of 20), conversation (6 of 20) and musical performance (4 of 20).

text.text: To understand how the learned dimensions related to the taxonomies captured in our pre-labeled annotations, we correlated the top learned dimensions with each of the pre-labeled annotations (Fig. 4).
text.formatted: To understand how the learned dimensions related to the taxonomies captured in our pre-labeled annotations, we correlated the top learned dimensions with each of the pre-labeled annotations (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">4</ref>).

text.text: We find that no single dimension maps one-to-one onto any single pre-labeled annotation.
While several dimensions correlate with prelabeled annotations, these often span visual, action/interaction, and social affective features.

A handful of dimensions (1: car conversation, 13: outdoor activities, 2: musical performance, and 6: cooking and eating) correlate weakly with action categories (r < 0.17), though the correlation is significant.
text.formatted: A handful of dimensions (1: car conversation, 13: outdoor activities, 2: musical performance, and 6: cooking and eating) correlate weakly with action categories (r < 0.17), though the correlation is significant.

text.text: Dimension 13 (outdoor activities) is the only dimension to correlate strongly with both scene annotations (Indoor/Outdoor = -0.61, Spatial Expanse = 0.63) indicating a less social-centric dimension.

Several dimensions correlate with social interaction or affective features (Dimensions: 1, 0, 13, 9, 2, 4, 3), while a few don't significantly correlate with any of the pre-labeled annotations (Dimensions 7, 17, 8).

Additionally, the annotations fail to separate dimensions that the learned embedding treats as distinct: caregiving (0) and infant-play (4) have nearly identical annotation profiles (r = 0.97), and while the two embeddings are correlated (r = 0.76) they rank largely different videos highest (3 of the top 20 videos shared, 3 of top 10 caption words shared), fractionating scenes that the annotations describe identically into distinct contexts.

This suggests that humans organize social videos flexibly among multiple scene properties, often combining information about social relationships and action categories in distinct ways not captured by simple linear combinations of these features.
Finally, we asked whether the learned similarity embedding predicts neural representational geometry.
Using independently collected fMRI data from the same study where participants (n = 4) viewed the same 250 videos [12] , we performed whole brain searchlight multiple regression RSA.
text.formatted: Using independently collected fMRI data from the same study where participants (n = 4) viewed the same 250 videos <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> , we performed whole brain searchlight multiple regression RSA.

text.text: In all four participants, the learned dimensions explained more variance than the annotations across occipitotemporal cortex (Fig. 5; Extended Data Fig. 6).
text.formatted: In all four participants, the learned dimensions explained more variance than the annotations across occipitotemporal cortex (Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">5</ref>; Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure">6</ref>).

text.text: The strongest effects lay on the lateral occipitotemporal surface, overlapping EBA and pSTS, and in ventral temporal cortex, indicating that the behaviorally derived structure is reflected in both lateral and ventral visual pathways.
The annotation model showed a weaker, more circumscribed pattern.
An advantage remained, although reduced, when the learned model was restricted to the 11 core dimensions, that is, to
To look with more statistical power, we also conducted analyses in functionally defined regions of interest (ROIs) along the lateral stream.
The learned dimensions explained more variance than the annotations in all lateral regions (Extended Data Fig. 8).
text.formatted: The learned dimensions explained more variance than the annotations in all lateral regions (Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure">8</ref>).

text.text: The advantage was largest in EVC, MT and EBA (∆r2 ≈ 0.2) and substantial in pSTS (∆r2 ≈ 0.18), but small in anterior STS (aSTS; ≈ 0.04), where the two models performed comparably and both remained well below the noise ceiling.

Finally, to understand how individual dimensions relate to responses across the visual cortex, we performed a winner-take-all searchlight analysis in which each voxel was labeled by the dimension (among the top 11) whose similarity structure correlated most strongly with the local neural RSM (Extended Data Fig. 9).
text.formatted: Finally, to understand how individual dimensions relate to responses across the visual cortex, we performed a winner-take-all searchlight analysis in which each voxel was labeled by the dimension (among the top 11) whose similarity structure correlated most strongly with the local neural RSM (Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure">9</ref>).

text.text: The best-predicting dimension varied across cortex, indicating that different regions are aligned with different aspects of the learned geometry.

Here we characterized the mental representations of dynamic social scenes directly from behavior, by learning an interpretable embedding to predict similarity judgments of naturalistic two person videos.
The embedding explained roughly twice as much behavioral variance as pre-labeled annotations derived from prior theories, and absorbed most of the variance the annotations explained.

Critically, these dimensions fractionate content that broad semantic categories and pre-labeled annotations collapse: infant-related scenes separated into caregiving, crying, and affectionate play rather than forming a single "baby" category.
Similarly, scenes depicting "play" are separated based on the participants and their social relationship (child-child versus parent-child).

The same dimensions predicted the representational geometry of the visual cortex, including the lateral pathway, better than the pre-labeled annotations, in fMRI data where participants passively viewed the videos, extending the significance of these dimensions beyond similarity judgments.
Together these results reveal a fine-grained organization of natural social scenes, combining social relationships and actions, that is shared across behavioral judgments and neural representations.
These results extend the data-driven embedding approach from static objects [17, 22] and isolated actions [20, 21, 27, 28] to dynamic, two-person interaction video clips.
text.formatted: These results extend the data-driven embedding approach from static objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">22]</ref> and isolated actions <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[20,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">27,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">28]</ref> to dynamic, two-person interaction video clips.

text.text: Prior work aimed at recovering the organizing dimensions of action representation more generally has uncovered relatively coarse social semantic, and action-related categories.
By focusing on two-person interactions, we identified nuanced distinctions among social events.
The fact that learned dimensions blend information about actions and social relationships highlights the importance of the underlying event structure and thematic roles (i.e., who did what to whom).

Such event role representations are central to human language, and recent work has highlighted their importance in visual narratives [29] and recent work suggests forms of this structure may be embedded in visual perception [10, 30] .
text.formatted: Such event role representations are central to human language, and recent work has highlighted their importance in visual narratives <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">[29]</ref> and recent work suggests forms of this structure may be embedded in visual perception <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">[10,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">30]</ref> .

text.text: This joint specification is not captured by trait axes, which describe relationships without activities, nor by action categories, which describe activities without relationships.
The short, de-contextualized nature of the video clips used may have emphasized a more visual or action-based feature space for participants [8] .
text.formatted: The short, de-contextualized nature of the video clips used may have emphasized a more visual or action-based feature space for participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8]</ref> .

text.text: However, features describing social relationships, namely intimacy and dominance, were the pre-annotated features that best predicted similarity judgments.

In the learned embeddings, these social-affective features were distributed across multiple dimensions, both positively and negatively (intimacy for example distinguished adult conversation versus caregiving and infant-play dimensions).
Surprisingly, action-related features were not strong standalone predictors of human similarity or the learned dimensions.
Even the full set of pre-labeled annotations based on prior action-based theories [6, 7, 12] was largely not predictive of the similarity space or learned embeddings.
text.formatted: Even the full set of pre-labeled annotations based on prior action-based theories <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">[6,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">12]</ref> was largely not predictive of the similarity space or learned embeddings.

text.text: Remarkably, the learned dimensions also matched neural data better than these action-based features, even in the lateral stream.

These findings are consistent with prior studies showing that lateral occipital regions correspond to behaviorally derived semantic structure [31, 32] , which suggest that information about social relationships may play a more important role in these regions than originally anticipated [8, 11, 13] .
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with prior studies showing that lateral occipital regions correspond to behaviorally derived semantic structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">[31,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">32]</ref> , which suggest that information about social relationships may play a more important role in these regions than originally anticipated <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">[8,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">11,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">13]</ref> .

text.text: Unlike other visual pathways, these lateral stream regions have also been difficult to predict with trained deep-network models [33] , underscoring that these behaviorally derived dimensions capture structure that current image-computable models cannot.
text.formatted: Unlike other visual pathways, these lateral stream regions have also been difficult to predict with trained deep-network models <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">[33]</ref> , underscoring that these behaviorally derived dimensions capture structure that current image-computable models cannot.

text.text: The learned dimensions are interpretable and reproducible (Extended Data Fig. 2), but one limitation is that their labels are based on video caption analysis and visual inspection.
text.formatted: The learned dimensions are interpretable and reproducible (Extended Data Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>), but one limitation is that their labels are based on video caption analysis and visual inspection.

text.text: Thus, an important open question is whether and how these features can be derived in a bottom-up, a priori manner.
Future work could collect participants' ratings for each dimension, as seen in prior work for objects [17] , to provide new taxonomies for social interactions.
text.formatted: Future work could collect participants' ratings for each dimension, as seen in prior work for objects <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> , to provide new taxonomies for social interactions.

text.text: Recent work has also shown that with fine-tuning, video foundation models can learn to reproduce this human social similarity structure [34] , suggesting a path forward for annotating new videos in an image-computable way.
text.formatted: Recent work has also shown that with fine-tuning, video foundation models can learn to reproduce this human social similarity structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> , suggesting a path forward for annotating new videos in an image-computable way.

text.text: Future work should test whether and how these approaches generalize to a wider set of new videos to see how these learned dimensions generalize across social contexts, populations, and stimulus sets.

Together, these findings show that the similarity structure of social scenes is highly nuanced and fine-grained, organized around novel combinations of actions and social relationships not captured by prior social-affective or action-based theories.
This work provides a compact set of behaviorally derived and neurally relevant dimensions for future studies of social representations in adults, throughout development, and in AI systems.
More generally, it provides a framework to extend data-driven representational spaces to increasingly complex and naturalistic social settings.
The stimulus set contained 250 short video clips (3 seconds each) displaying naturalistic social interactions [12] .
text.formatted: The stimulus set contained 250 short video clips (3 seconds each) displaying naturalistic social interactions <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> .

text.text: The selected clips came from the Moments in Time dataset [5] .
text.formatted: The selected clips came from the Moments in Time dataset <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">[5]</ref> .

text.text: The aim of this selection was to enforce a requirement of two-person interactions across varying relationship types (e.g., friends, strangers, parent-child), activities (e.g., conversation, playing, eating, task collaboration), emotional tone (e.g., friendly, adversarial, neutral), and setting (indoors vs. outdoors; private vs. public spaces).
The stimuli contained no audio to eliminate cues related to spoken language.
Participants totaled N = 232, recruited from an online university crowd-sourcing platform and were awarded course credits for participation.
The triplet odd-oneout experiment was hosted and collected similarity judgments through the Meadows Research platform (https://meadows-research.com).
text.formatted: The triplet odd-oneout experiment was hosted and collected similarity judgments through the Meadows Research platform (<ref type="url" target="https://meadows-research.com">https://meadows-research.com</ref>).

text.text: All participants gave informed consent, and data was collected under the JHU Homewood Institutional Review Board (IRB) approval.

In addition to the similarity judgments, captions describing each video were previously collected from a different set of participants, which we use to facilitate content and learned dimension analysis.
Each participant completed a set of at least 220 trials in which three videos were simultaneously presented in a random arrangement on a web-based interface.
The instruction for each trial was "From each triplet, please choose the one you feel is the odd-one-out.".
This forced-choice paradigm reveals perceptual similarity structure by indicating which two of the three stimuli are judged as most alike [17, 35] .
text.formatted: This forced-choice paradigm reveals perceptual similarity structure by indicating which two of the three stimuli are judged as most alike <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">35]</ref> .

text.text: Two sets of participants and trials were collected: 215 participants judged 49,484 triplets of the 250 videos used as a training and validation set. 17 additional participants judged 3,739 triplets of a 50 video subset (pre-determined test stimuli), used for held-out evaluation.

Only a small fraction of possible triplets can be sampled (49,484 of 2,573,000 for 250 videos; 3,739 of 19,600 for 50 videos), so triplets were chosen using a greedy setcover selection algorithm [34] to cover pairs rather than triplets: every pair of videos co-occurs in at least one triplet, with on average ∼4 judgments per pair in the training set and ∼9 in the test set.
text.formatted: Only a small fraction of possible triplets can be sampled (49,484 of 2,573,000 for 250 videos; 3,739 of 19,600 for 50 videos), so triplets were chosen using a greedy setcover selection algorithm <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">[34]</ref> to cover pairs rather than triplets: every pair of videos co-occurs in at least one triplet, with on average ∼4 judgments per pair in the training set and ∼9 in the test set.

text.text: Unlike probabilistic random sampling [17] , this achieves complete pairwise coverage at a smaller triplet count.
text.formatted: Unlike probabilistic random sampling <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> , this achieves complete pairwise coverage at a smaller triplet count.

text.text: This was a deliberate design trade that maximizes reliable RSM estimation per judgment for a stimulus set of this size.
Each set of trials included catch trials in which one video appeared twice alongside a different video; the correct response was the non-repeated video.
Participants who selected the repeated video on any catch trial were excluded from all analyses (n = 30).
The final sample had a mean age of 19.5 years; 148 participants identified as female, 76 as male, 2 as non-binary, and 6 did not report gender.
In terms of ethnicity, 78.0% identified as not Hispanic or Latino and 19.0% as Hispanic or Latino, with 3% not reporting ethnicity.
In terms of race, 39.2% identified as Asian, 36.2% as White, 10.8% as Black, 4.7% as more than one race, 3.9% as other, and 0.4% as American Indian, with 4.7% not reporting race.
A Representational Similarity Matrix (RSM) was created using the pairwise judgments from the collected held-out triplets utilizing the probabilities of choices and the counts of judged pairs.
In reporting we utilize a split-half reliability metric to estimate the noise ceiling of the human judgments.

Specifically, we randomly split the triplet judgments into two halves, construct a separate representational similarity matrix (RSM) from each half, and compute the Spearman correlation between the upper triangles of the two RSMs (restricted to pairs with at least one observation in both halves).

This procedure is repeated over 1,000 random splits and the mean half-length correlation is corrected using the Spearman-Brown corrected formula, r SB = 2r/(1 + r), to estimate the reliability of the held-out dataset.
The resulting value serves as a noise ceiling, representing the maximum correlation any model could be expected to achieve given the variability in human responses.
To model the mental representation of the videos, we trained a sparse positive similarity embedding (SPoSE) [17] model optimized to predict the triplet choices observed in human participants.
text.formatted: To model the mental representation of the videos, we trained a sparse positive similarity embedding (SPoSE) <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> model optimized to predict the triplet choices observed in human participants.

text.text: The model represents each video as a non-negative point in a D-dimensional space, initially set to D = 90 as an overcomplete basis.
We employed a triplet-loss learning method similar to that described by Hebart et al [17].
text.formatted: We employed a triplet-loss learning method similar to that described by Hebart et al <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref>.

text.text: For a triplet (i, j, k), the similarity of each pair was defined as the dot product of their embedding vectors.
The probability that a given pair was judged most similar, with the remaining video as the odd one out, was the softmax of the three pairwise similarities.
The model was trained to minimize the negative log-likelihood of the human choices, plus an L1 penalty on the embedding weights to promote sparsity (λ = 0.01).
The penalty was ramped up linearly from 0 to its full value over the first 20 epochs, which lets the embedding first fit the choice data before sparsity is imposed.
Optimization used Adam (learning rate = 0.001, β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, ϵ = 10 -7 ) with a mini-batch size of 100 triplets, and the training data were reshuffled every epoch.
The triplet dataset was split at random at the triplet level: 90% of judgments (44,535) were used for training and 10% (4,949) for validation.
Training ran for at most 200 epochs, with early stopping when validation accuracy did not improve by at least 0.0005 for 20 consecutive epochs.
After training, dimensions were pruned following Hebart et al. [17] : any dimension whose maximum activation across all 250 videos was below 0.1 was removed.
text.formatted: After training, dimensions were pruned following Hebart et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> : any dimension whose maximum activation across all 250 videos was below 0.1 was removed.

text.text: This left 40 dimensions.
Top dimension selection used only training-set 10-fold cross-validated r 2 ; the Kneedle elbow [26] was identified on this training curve and fixed before any evaluation of the held-out test RSM.
text.formatted: Top dimension selection used only training-set 10-fold cross-validated r 2 ; the Kneedle elbow <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">[26]</ref> was identified on this training curve and fixed before any evaluation of the held-out test RSM.

text.text: Of the pruned 40 dimensions, approximately 11 were identified as a core interpretable subset that best explains the similarity judgments, as described in the Results.

All primary analyses, including the explained variance of human similarity judgments and neural comparisons, use the full 40-dimension embedding, unless otherwise stated, while the top 11 dimensions are used for visualization and interpretability.

We used the twelve pre-labeled annotations released with the stimulus set [12] : spatial expanse, indoor/outdoor, inter-agent distance, agents facing, object-directed action, acting jointly, communication, cooperation, dominance, intimacy, valence and arousal.
text.formatted: We used the twelve pre-labeled annotations released with the stimulus set <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> : spatial expanse, indoor/outdoor, inter-agent distance, agents facing, object-directed action, acting jointly, communication, cooperation, dominance, intimacy, valence and arousal.

text.text: Each continuous feature was rated by at least 10 online participants per video on a five-point Likert scale and averaged across raters; indoor/outdoor is a binary label.
For each feature we built an RSM over the test videos whose entries are one minus the Euclidean distance.
Rater reliability for these annotations is reported in McMahon et al [12] .
text.formatted: Rater reliability for these annotations is reported in McMahon et al <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> .

text.text: A thirteenth, action-category RSM was built from each video's Moments in Time label, with two videos counted as similar if they share a category, 0 otherwise.
To evaluate pre-labeled annotations and learned dimensions, we constructed models predicting similarity using multiple regression RSA [24, 25] .
text.formatted: To evaluate pre-labeled annotations and learned dimensions, we constructed models predicting similarity using multiple regression RSA <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[24,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">25]</ref> .

text.text: Predictors (13 annotation RSMs, or the 40 and top 11 dimension similarity vectors) were entered into an ordinary-least-squares regression predicting the upper triangle of the held-out 50-video human RSM.
Model fit was evaluated with 10-fold cross-validation over stimulus pairs (5 repeats) as the squared Spearman correlation between out-of-fold predictions and observed similarities.
Because the predictors are fixed stimulus properties and only one weight per predictor is estimated, pair-level folds do not fit stimulus-specific parameters.
Unique variance for a predictor set was the full-model r 2 minus the r 2 of the model without that set; shared variance was the remainder.

Significance was assessed by permuting the video labels of the human RSM (1,000 permutations) and Bonferronicorrecting across two families: pre-labeled annotations and 8 summary tests (model totals and variance-partition terms) in Fig. 2.
text.formatted: Significance was assessed by permuting the video labels of the human RSM (1,000 permutations) and Bonferronicorrecting across two families: pre-labeled annotations and 8 summary tests (model totals and variance-partition terms) in Fig. <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">2</ref>.

text.text: Confidence intervals were obtained by a video-level bootstrap: on each of 1,000 iterations the 50 test videos were resampled with replacement, pairs of a video with itself were discarded, and all models were refit with the same cross-validation, with folds grouped by original video pair so that duplicated pairs never appeared in both training and test folds.
Intervals are 2.5th-97.5th percentiles.
To interpret the learned dimensions, we examined how video examples were distributed across the embedding.
For each of the top 11 dimensions, we selected the eight videos with the highest activations in each dimension and visually and semantically identified common themes.
We also analyzed the video captions within dimensions.
For each dimension, we compared caption word frequencies between the 8 highest and 8 lowest loading videos.
Each word was scored with a smoothed log ratio, log (︁ (n high + 0.5)/(n low + 0.5) )︁ , weighted by log(n high + n low + 1) to down-weight rare words.
The top 20 words with positive log ratios were retained and reported as word clouds with font-size scaled by log ratio, for each dimension to aid interpretation and labeling.
We additionally calculated Jensen-Shannon divergence (bits) between the full caption word distributions of the 8 highest and 8 lowest loading videos, averaged over 200 random tie-breaks.
Significance was assessed against a null of 5,000 random disjoint 8-video pairs (mean 0.61 bits).
We also compared fMRI data from a separate group of 4 healthy young adults.
These data were collected in a previous study [12] ; all participants provided written informed consent, and the study was approved by the Johns Hopkins University Institutional Review Board.
text.formatted: These data were collected in a previous study <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">[12]</ref> ; all participants provided written informed consent, and the study was approved by the Johns Hopkins University Institutional Review Board.

text.text: During scanning, participants viewed all 250 video clips in random order across multiple runs using a rapid event-related design, with each clip repeated 9-10 times for the 200 training clips and 18-20 times for the 50 test clips.
Regions of interest (ROIs) were defined anatomically and supplemented with functional localizers of the lateral stream: EVC, MT, LOC, EBA, pSTS, and aSTS.
We performed whole-brain searchlight RSA using a 3-voxel radius sphere centered on each reliable voxel.
For each searchlight sphere, we constructed a local neural RSM from the Pearson correlation distances between the 50 test stimuli.
We evaluated two complementary searchlight analyses:

Within each sphere, we regressed the local neural RSM onto two predictor sets in separate models: the 40 learned dimensions (and 11 in a supplemental experiment) and 13 pre-labeled annotations (12 behavioral and 1 action category).
Each model was fit with 10-fold cross-validation over the 50 test stimuli.
We computed cross-validated Spearman correlation squared (r 2 ) with the observed local RSM.

This produced, for every sphere, a full-model r 2 (all predictors jointly) and a unique r 2 for each individual predictor, computed as the difference between the full model and a model omitting that predictor (r 2 full -r 2 leave-one-out ).
text.formatted: This produced, for every sphere, a full-model r 2 (all predictors jointly) and a unique r 2 for each individual predictor, computed as the difference between the full model and a model omitting that predictor (r <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">2</ref> full -r 2 leave-one-out ).

text.text: Per subject, we visualized the combined full-model map on that subject's own native FreeSurfer inflated surface.
Within each searchlight sphere, we computed the Spearman correlation between the local neural RSM and the similarity vector of each of the top 11 learned dimensions individually (marginal r).
Each voxel was assigned the label of the dimension with the highest r, and voxels where no dimension exceeded r > 0.1 were left unlabeled.
text.formatted: Each voxel was assigned the label of the dimension with the highest r, and voxels where no dimension exceeded r > 0.1 were left unlabeled.

text.text: Voxelwise maps were projected onto each subject's FreeSurfer inflated cortical surface, and surface faces were colored by the majority label of their vertices.
In addition, for each ROI localizer, neural RSMs were constructed by computing Pearson correlation between voxel patterns for each pair of videos.

Using a similar multiple regression RSA approach as before, we predicted the upper triangle of each neural RSM using the pre-labeled annotations and learned dimensions and compared using Spearman rank correlation squared (r 2 ).
The noise ceiling was calculated using the method described in Nili et al [36] .
text.formatted: The noise ceiling was calculated using the method described in Nili et al <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">[36]</ref> .

text.text: The lower bound is the mean Spearman r 2 between each subject's RSM and the mean of the other subjects (leave-one-out); the upper bound is the mean Spearman r 2 between each subject's RSM and the mean of all subjects (including themselves).

To evaluate the stability of the embedding dimensions, we retrained the model 20 times under two perturbations: random re-initialization (seed) on the same triplets and retraining on triplets resampled with replacement to the same size (bootstrap).
Following the procedure of Hebart et al. [17] : each reference dimension was matched to whichever retrained column correlated most highly with it.
text.formatted: Following the procedure of Hebart et al. <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">[17]</ref> : each reference dimension was matched to whichever retrained column correlated most highly with it.

text.text: The correlations across dimensions were Fisher z-transformed, averaged, and back-transformed to a mean reliability, separately for seed and bootstrap retrains.
Dimensions were considered recoverable if they surpassed a threshold value of r = 0.6-the threshold Hebart et al. used to report dimension reliability.

To confirm this threshold is not attributable to chance given the limited number of candidate columns per retrain (40 pruned dimensions), we built a null distribution by shuffling each reference dimension's video correspondence before matching (500 permutations); the null mean reliability never exceeded r = 0.26, confirming this threshold is far above chance.
Fractionation reproducibility was measured on independent retrains of the embedding.
For each of the 20 bootstrap retrains, we selected 11 dimensions from that retrain's own embedding using the same greedy forward cumulative approach described above.
Each selected dimension was matched to its closest-correlating (Pearson r) reported dimension across all 250 videos.
A reported dimension was classified as fractionated in a given retrain when two or more of that retrain's selected dimensions matched it above a floor of 0.3 (99.7th percentile of permutation null).

For each classified pair we computed shared top-20 videos, shared top-10 contrastive caption words, and Pearson r, and retained only pairs closer to the reported caregiving/infantplay example (r = 0.76, 3/20, 3/10) than to a true-merge control (r = 1.0, 20/20, 10/10)-shared videos ≤ 11, shared words ≤ 6, r < 0.8.
text.formatted: For each classified pair we computed shared top-20 videos, shared top-10 contrastive caption words, and Pearson r, and retained only pairs closer to the reported caregiving/infantplay example (r = 0.76, 3/20, 3/10) than to a true-merge control (r = 1.0, 20/20, 10/10)-shared videos ≤ 11, shared words ≤ 6, r < 0.8.

text.text: This study was not preregistered.

Sample size was not determined by a power analysis; instead, the number of triplets was fixed in advance by the pairwise coverage criterion described in Section 4.2, which ensured every video pair co-occurred in at least one triplet (∼4 judgments per pair for the 250-video training set, 215 participants; ∼9 per pair for the 50-video test set, 17 participants).
The number of participants followed from the number of triplets required, given that each participant completed at least 220 trials.

Fig 1 Methods overview. (a) We collected a new dataset of triplet judgments from 250 3-second videos of everyday 2-person events.
Participants were asked to select "which video was the odd one out?"

Two experiments were conducted, the first to collect the training and validation set of triplets (49,484) and later to collect a held-out set of test triplets (3,739). (b) A SPoSE model was trained on a training set of triplets, to make a prediction of the odd one out.

This prediction was compared to the human choice and model weights were updated (see Methods, Section 4.3). (c) Pre-labeled annotations released with the dataset were converted into RSMs and compared to the similarity probability matrix using multiple regression RSA.

Fig 2 Predicting similarity judgments with pre-labeled annotations and learned dimensions. (a) Total variance explained by each pre-labeled annotation individually in a multipleregression RSA, alongside the total explained by all 13 annotations jointly (rightmost bar). (b) Total variance explained by all 40 learned dimensions, and by the top 11 dimensions. (c) Combined model of the pre-labeled annotations and the 40 learned dimensions, decomposed into variance unique to each set and variance shared between them; the square marker denotes the total of the combined model, with its 95% CI shown beside the bar.
Error bars show 95% confidence intervals from a video-level bootstrap (1,000 resamples of the 50 test videos).
Dashed gray line: split-half reliability of the heldout human judgments (Spearman-Brown corrected), used as a noise ceiling; the shaded band is its 95% CI.
Asterisks indicate p ≤ 0.05 by permutation test (1,000 permutations), Bonferroni-corrected.
Fig.3Interpreting learned dimensions.
The top 11 dimensions that explain the most cumulative variance in similarity judgments, illustrated with their most strongly associated stimuli.

Each row represents a dimension, with rows sorted by greedy predictive performance (Methods, Section 4.3), and the columns show a frame from each of the 8 videos with the highest activations on that dimension.

Next to each dimension is a word cloud of the 20 most contrastive words from human-written captions of those 8 videos, colored by part of speech: noun (blue), verb (green), adjective (red), adverb (purple) and other (gray).
Word size is scaled by contrastive log ratio, with larger words being more contrastive.
